Furthermore the overwriting of existing files requires additional permission from the user on a per-file basis, as does the running of expressions.
The intensity or purity of a colour, ranging from a neutral grey at zero to a fully saturated chromatic value at one.
A field which associates a number with every point in space. In physics, scalar refers to a unitless number.

The multiplication of a vector and a number. The result is a single vector whose length equals the length of the original vector times the number input. When a vector is multiplied by a negative number, it changes direction as well as magnitude.
See _Dilation_.
A free-form text annotation on the [GH] canvas, used for commenting and labelling.
The portion of a closed shape where its two extreme ends meet and form the loop required for the shape to be closed.
A trigonometric function operating on angles in right-angled triangles. The secant of an angle equals the ratio of the hypotenuse to the adjacent edge.

In computing, an integer used as the initial state of a random number generator. The seed controls the first number in a pseudo-random sequence, this first number is then modified by the algorithm to generate the next number and so on.
A section of geometry bounded by distinct edges or end points.

In mathematics, a set is an unordered collection of unique elements. Sets may be finite, e.g. all the 10-digit primes, or infinite, e.g. all the ways in which I love you. Sets are even allowed to contain themselves. For example, the set of all concepts is, itself, a concept.
See\: Crease Edge

A geometric transformation in which all the points in a plane, parallel to the transformation base plane, move together. How far the points move is directly proportional to their distance from the base plane. Turning a rectangle into a parallellogram, or a box into a parallellopiped is an example of shearing.
A state of the Preview property in which the data from a [GH] object is shown in the [RH] viewports.
Adjective used to describe functions which smoothly transition from one value to another. Common sigmoid functions available in [GH] include `atan`, `tanh`, `erf`, `logistic` and `smooth step`.

An area metric with support for negative values. For example, the sign of the area of a region may depend on the orientation of its boundary, i.e. whether the boundary runs clockwise or anticlockwise. This is commonly used to define holes in regions, as the negative area of a hole is automatically subtracted from the total area of the region.

A distance metric which supports negative values. For example, a point underneath a plane can be said to have a negative distance to that plane. Similarly, the sign of a distance can be used to indicate whether a point is located inside or outside of a shape.
A length metric with support for negative values. For example, an interval will have a negative length, if its initial value is larger than its final value.

A volume metric with support for negative values. For example, the sign of the volume of a shape may be negative if the shape is turned inside out. This may be intentional in the case of holes or voids, but it may also result from misaligned normals.
A trigonometric function operating on angles in right-angled triangles. The sine of an angle equals the ratio of the opposite edge to the hypotenuse.

A type of floating point number which uses 32 bits in total. This is the most commonly used number type in display-related programming. When written in a decimal format, single precision floating point numbers have about 6 to 9 significant decimal places.
An interval where the end value equals the start value. As the length of an interval is calculated by subtracting the start value from the end value, a singleton interval has a zero length.
A graph node which can be entered but not left, because all its edges are one-way edges pointing towards it. Once a sink has been reached, no other node can be visited.

A type of distance metric showing the distance between two colours in the H*SP sinusoidal model. Unlike in the cylindrical model, the poles representing pure white and black are pinched into points. This metric corresponds to the human experience of colour better than the other hue-saturation metrics, in that the hue difference in very light and very dark values is suppressed. E.g. strong blue and strong red are shown as being farther apart from each other than very dark blue and very dark red.

The combination of a _path_ and an _index_ designating the exact location of an item within a data tree. The path portion of a site specifies the twig within the tree, and the index specifies the item within that twig.
A measure of the asymmetry in a statistical distribution or a collection of samples. Distributions which are symmetrical around the mean have no skewness.
See\: Tangent Edge
A common interpolation function defined on the interval [0, 1]. The SmoothStep function is a sigmoid, or S-shaped, cubic polynomial with horizontal tangents at both zero and one.

A type of colour interpolation used in colour gradients. The colour of any given gradient location is a smooth combination of the colours of the grips on either side. This interpolation yields a smoother progression across grips than the linear interpolation scheme.
An interpolation function defined on the interval [0, 1]. The SmootherStep function is a sigmoid, or S-shaped, degree 5 polynomial with horizontal tangents at both zero and one.
An interpolation function defined on the interval [0, 1]. The SmoothestStep function is a sigmoid, or S-shaped, degree 7 polynomial with horizontal tangents at both zero and one.
See 'Yank'.
A difference involving two or more closed surfaces or meshes.
An intersection involving two or more closed surfaces or meshes.
A union involving two or more closed surfaces or meshes.

In [GH], solutions refer both to the computed data associated with a specific file and the process of computing that data. Whenever a file is modified, e.g. by adding or removing a component, by creating or deleting a wire, or by modifying the state of an existing component, the current solution expires and the calculations required for the new solution begin.
The numeric or textual proxies representing the property on which a sorting of values is based. For example, when sorting curves from short to long, the lengths are used as the sort keys.

In programming, an ordered collection of unique values, which are always in ascending order. Finding a value in a sorted list is faster than finding one in an unsorted list, but adding a value is slower.
Reordering a list so that all items are placed in ascending order. Two types exist; numeric and textual. Of these two, textual sorting is culture dependent.
A graph node which can be left but not entered, because all its edges are one-way edges pointing away from it. It is impossible to reach a source when starting from any other node.
A subdomain of a NURBS curve or surface bounded by two consecutive knots. A span represents a portion of a NURBS shape which can be described using a single polynomial equation.
In [RH], a closed surface defined by a base plane and a radius.
A coordinate system which describes the location of points on or around a sphere using a radius and two angles.

A planar curve that winds around a fixed centre at a consistently increasing distance. Different growth functions yield spirals of different types. The most common of these are Circular for zero growth, Archimedean for linear growth, and Constant Pitch for exponential growth spirals.
In CAD, a type of curve defined by polynomial functions. In [RH] these are predominantly referred to as _curves_.
In statistics, a way to describe how spread out or concentrated the observations in a sample are.
In geometry, a unit of angle measurement originating in the field of rational trigonometry. Unlike with degrees and radians, simple addition can not be used to add two spread values together.
An implementation of the RGB colour model, which differs from linear RGB in that it compresses the dark colours. This allows for a greater number of bright colours.

A type of distance metric showing the distance between two colours in the `sRGB` unit cube. Identical colours have a distance of zero, while the largest possible distance between colours equals $\\sqrt{3}$, signifying the distance between the opposite corners of the colour cube.

An attribute of sorting algorithms, indicating that values retain their original order provided this does not conflict with the sort order. E.g. values which are identical with respect to sort order are not shuffled.
In programming, a collection of values, of which the only accessible or removable element is the last one. Adding a value to a stack is called _pushing_, and removing one is called _popping_.
In mathematics, the field of study concerned with collecting, organising, analysing,  and interpretating data.

A [GH] object property, which determines whether or not a [GH] object is enabled or disabled, i.e. on or off. The status of an object can be set through the menus. Changing the status causes all the dependent objects to recalculate.

A type of continuous distribution modelling the distribution of an entire population, when only a sample of the population is known. Unlike the normal distribution, the T-distribution takes into account the size of the known sample. Especially for small sample sizes, the resulting curve has fatter tails and a lower peak than the normal distribution curve, reflecting the increased uncertainty within the calculation.
See\: Subdivision Surface

A type of surface defined as the mathematical limit of an infinite sequence of subdivisions of a control mesh. Subdivision surfaces, or SubDs for short, are one of the fundamental types of surfaces in [RH] and [GH], and they are uniquely suited for organic and curved shapes.

The process of refining a discrete shape into a smoother and denser one. This is almost always done by inserting new vertices in between existing ones, and subsequently updating the connecting faces and edges. [GH] provides several ways to subdivide polylines and meshes.
In [RH] and [GH], a type of surface defined by sliding a profile curve along a path curve.
In mathematics, any two-dimensional object in a two or higher-dimensional space.
A property of a shape, meaning it is invariant under one or more transformations, such as rotation, translation, and especially reflection.

The default [.NET] pseudorandom generator and the only one available in [GH] 1. Although fast, reliable and commonly available, the System generator will produce obvious patterns in three or more sequences, whose seed values differ by basic ratios. The System generator belongs to the _Linear Congruential_ algorithm family.

An edge whose adjacent faces have parallel normals along the entire length of the edge. Tangent edges are also sometimes called smooth edges, because the transition from one face to another is smooth.

The hyperbolic tangent function defined as the ratio between `sinh` and `cosh`. The hyperbolic tangent is a sigmoid function with a domain covering the entire number line, and a co-domain from -1 to +1.
A geometric transformation mimicking the effects of one, two or three point perspectives.

An approximation of an arbitrary, continuous function constructed out of a sequence of polynomial terms, which are based on the derivative of said underlying function. Taylor series are a method to convert a function into polynomial form, making it more suitable or efficient for certain tasks.
A function or operator of arity three, e.g. `clip(x,a,b)` or the conditional operator `if a, then b, else c`.

The act of covering a surface in a regular grid of non-overlapping shapes, which are identical or similar to each other. Common tesselations can be created using triangles, squares, rectangles, and hexagons, but other shapes and mixtures of shapes can also form valid tesselations.
A type of annotation geometry placed in [RH] by [GH], primarily consisting of a point location and a text segment. The font and colour properties of text dots can be overridden using [GH] meta data.
Any sequence of characters. In programming this is commonly known as a _string_. Text with zero characters is called an _empty string_.
A combination of various date and time properties appended to file names when files are backed up during a save action.
The level of accuracy, below which differences are treated as equalities.
In mathematics, the field of study concerned with the classification and connectedness of shapes.

A measure of a curve's local non-planarity. Torsion describes how quickly the curve departs from the curvature plane. Note that it is possible to have curvature without any torsion, if the curve is locally planar, as is the case for circles and spirals, but it is not possible to have torsion without curvature.
In [RH], a closed surface defined by a base plane, a major radius and a minor radius. May also be known as "doughnut".
See\: Transformation
A $4 \\times 4$ matrix which describes any combination of transformations.

In mathematics and CAD, a change made to a shape in which all straight lines remain straight after the change. No lines are bent, broken or cut. Examples include _translation_, _rotation_, _reflection_ and _dilation_.
A graph node which can be both entered and left. Two-way edges count as both incoming and outgoing edges. A transit node connected by only a single two-way edge is called a cul-de-sac.
A ternary function which allows for the smooth transition from one function to another.
A geometric transformation where a shape is moved in a single direction for a specified distance.
An aspect of colour or material denoting how well one can see through it.

The way in which data is stored throughout [GH]. Trees are sorted collections of _twigs_, the ordering of which is determined by their associated _paths_. The twigs contain the actual data, while the paths specify both the sorting order of, and relatedness between twigs.
See _Triangle_.
A mesh facet connecting three vertices.

A type of continuous distribution with a finite range, where the probability of outcomes increases from zero at the start and end of the range, to maximum at the mode. Mostly used in cases of scarce data and unlikely to represent the results of natural processes.

In geometry, to cover a surface in a patchwork of non-overlapping triangles which together provide a discrete approximation of the underlying surface. If the triangulation is regular, it may be considered a tesselation.
A collection of adjacent triangles whose corners are coincident with a given collection of points, without gaps or overlaps.
The approximation of a surface with a collection of adjacent triangles, without gaps or overlaps.
In mathematics, a field of geometry which studies relationships of angles and lengths in triangles.
A boundary curve for a surface, used to remove unwanted regions.

A cone shape with the tip sliced off. Truncated cones have two parallel, circular capping surfaces at the top and the bottom. If the radius of the top and bottom caps are equal, the shape becomes a cylinder.

A primitive surface type in [GH] 2.0, alongside spheres, boxes and planes. Tubes are defined by a central, finite axis, two radii at either end, and a wall thickness, measured inwards. By picking these properties carefully tubes can resemble solid and open cones, solid and open cylinders as well as truncated cones.
In geometry, a unit of angle measurement. A full circle equals 1. Turns are most commonly used in programming.
In [GH], ordered collections of items. Each item is addressed by an index, starting at zero for the first one. Optional meta data may be associated with the individual items.
In [GH], the understanding of and the skill set applied to the analysis and modification of data trees.
A graph edge which allows travel from its start node to its end node and vice versa. One-way edges only allow travel in the forward direction.

A categorisation of data according to how it is treated by [GH]. This categorisation does not necessarily follow from the contents of the data themselves. E.g. points and vectors both consist of a triplet of numbers, yet they belong to different types. Whether a number triplet is treated as a point or a vector is determined by the type it belongs to.

A type of continuous distribution which is only defined between two limit values, and where the values close to the limit are far more likely than those in the middle of the range. Higher $U$ powers push the values further outwards.
A function or operator of arity one, e.g. `cos(x)` or the square root.
A dilation transformation in which the scaling factor is the same in all directions.
See _Uniform Dilation_.
A vector with the length of one unit. In mathematical notation, unit vectors will often be denoted with a hat diacritic\: `û`.
To remove some or all of the custom boundary curves of a trimmed surface, restoring its full, intrinsic shape.
URIs, or universal resource identifiers, are the most generic ways in which computers locate files or other data. They support both web-based URLs as well as files and directories on local discs.
A URL, or uniform resource locator, specifies the location of a resource on a computer network.
The number of times a value appears in a collection, or the number of elements converging in one place.
An instance of a data type. For example _colour_ would be a type, while _purple_ would be a value of that type. An absence of a value is called _null_.
In statistics, variance describes the expected squared deviation of any value from the mean of a distribution.
An extension of numeric algebra which adds vectors and matrices as value types.
A field which associates a three-dimensional vector with every point in space. Can be used e.g. to model velocity of wind or the force of a magnet.
Multiplication in vector algebra. The two types of vector product are the _cross product_ and the _dot product_.

A direction and magnitude in space. An individual vector is defined by a set of numbers, which denote its length along the principal directions of a coordinate system. Its magnitude is $\\left\\| v \\right\\| = \\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$.
The most detailed level of logging. All messages are included in the log file.
Colours associated with individual mesh vertices. Not to be confused with material colours.
A single point which is a part of a larger geometrical shape.

A numeric value which exceeds the 1~10 million range can be considered very large and may cause computational issues. Due to the way in which decimal numbers are stored on digital computers, mathematics with big values becomes less accurate. The rounding gaps between possible distinct number values grows as the number magnitude gets bigger, and eventually those gaps will become comparable to the tolerances [RH] uses, compromising reliability of operations.
Data which emerges from the [GH] file as it runs. Volatile data does not survive the saving of a file, therefore it must be recomputed every time the file is opened.

A single region in a Voronoi partition, consisting of all the points nearest to one seed point. The phrase Voronoi cell may also refer to the boundary of the region, such as a convex polyline in the 2-dimensional case or a convex polyhedron in the 3-dimensional case.

A partition of space into regions, where each region contains all the points closest to a particular seed point. Unweighted Voronoi partitions consist of a collection of non-overlapping, convex polyhedra, which together fully cover the underlying space.

The three-dimensional analogue of a pixel. I.e. a single value in an orthogonal, volumetric grid of values. Voxels may contain a variety of values, including Booleans, numbers, or colours, depending on the use case at hand.

In [GH], a category of feedback messages indicating a possible mistake. The operation still yields a result, but possibly not the desired one. Objects with warnings are colour-coded along their top edges.
The distance between two adjacent peaks -or throughs- in a wave.  Wavelength is the arithmetic inverse of frequency.
A type of continuous distribution modelling lifetime expectancy based on failure rates.

A property of the control points of NURBS curves and surfaces. When different control points belonging to the same shape have different weights, the final shape is locally pulled towards the control points with higher weights.
A programming loop which repeats until a specific condition is either fulfilled or violated.

A pseudorandom number generator in the _Combined Multiplicative Congruential_ algorithm family, published in 2006 by B. A. Wichmann and I.D. Hill, which improves upon their earlier algorithm from 1982.

A pseudorandom number generator in the _Combined Multiplicative Congruential_ algorithm family, published in 1982 by B. A. Wichmann and I.D. Hill. The purpose of this algorithm was to create pseudorandom sequences with much longer cycles by stacking three regular random generators with differing cycle lengths on top of each other.
In computation, a type of data conversion in which no information is lost.
A type of continuous distribution with a limited range, where the probabilities of outcomes form the upper half of an ellipse going from the start to the end of the range.

The primary mechanism for sharing data amongst different objects in a [GH] file. Wires always connect the output of one parameter with the input of another parameter, thus establishing data inheritance.
The collection of all curves covering the edges and prominent isocurves of a surface or mesh.
The full name of the virtual, red-like colour primary in the `XYZ` colour model. We made this one up.
A high performance family of pseudorandom number generators published by G. Marsaglia in 2003. It is the fastest generator in the _Well Equidistributed Long-Period Linear_ algorithm family.

A high quality, high speed pseudorandom number generator. The specific implementation in [GH] is the Xoshiro256**, as published by D. Blackman and S. Vigna in 2018. The algorithm is named after its principal operations eXclusive-Or, Shift and Rotate and represents a different -and generally better- approach to pseudorandom sequences than both the _Linear Congruential_ and _Well Equidistributed Long-Period Linear_ algorithm families.

A mathematically transformed implementation of the RGB colour model. Instead of the red, green and blue primaries heavily implied by the RGB model, the XYZ colour space defines imaginary primaries called `X`, `Y` and `Z` which are not physically possible. By selecting primaries well outside the scope of all real colours, it becomes possible to represent all humanly visible colours by linearly interpolating the primaries.
A characteristic of curves and surfaces calculated with the fourth derivative.
The full name of the virtual, green-like colour primary in the `XYZ` colour model. We made this one up.

An implementation of the luma-chroma colour model, strictly speaking defined as a transformation of the `XYZ` colour space. The `Y` axis represents the luminance, while the `x` and `y` axes encode the chrominance aspect of a colour, although not in as obvious a way as the `a` and `b` axes in the `L*a*b*` colour space. When plotted at a constant `Y` value, the `Yxy` space yields what is commonly called the _CIE Chromaticity diagram_.

A type of discrete distribution describing the ubiquity and rarity of values in a data set. E.g. the frequency of words in a language form a Zipf distribution, with a few words such as "the" and "you" occurring very frequently, a somewhat larger group of words which occur fairly regularly such as "chair" and "watch", but with the majority of words being very rare, such as "sonorous" or "latibule". The full name of the virtual, blue-like colour primary in the `XYZ` colour model. We made this one up.
